pNFS overview

  • Parallel NFS (pNFS) is an extension of the NFSv4.1 protocol designed to significantly improve throughput for NFS workloads by enabling clients to perform data reads and writes directly and concurrently to multiple nodes within a cluster, rather than routing all I/O through a single NFS server.

    In a traditional NFS deployment, a client mounts a share and directs all read and write operations to the single node associated with the mount IP address, which inherently limits performance and creates a bottleneck regardless of overall cluster size or capability.

    Figure 15.    Regular NFS client mount to a single PowerScale node.

    All I/O for this mount is between the client and node over NFSv3 or NFSv4.1, while the remainer of the cluster’s nodes sit idle for this client.

    In contrast, when pNFS is enabled in OneFS 9.15 and later, the client continues to communicate with a single node on the cluster for metadata operations such as file open, close, rename, and attribute queries, but is explicitly informed which other nodes to send the actual file data to.

    Figure 16.    Parallel NFS (pNFS) client mount to multiple PowerScale cluster nodes.

    Any node in the cluster can act as the metadata server (MDS) or serve data connections (DS). This separation of the metadata path from the data path allows file I/O traffic to be distributed across multiple nodes in the cluster, thereby maximizing available bandwidth and parallelism.

    In a pNFS-enabled storage cluster, the client always talks to the MDS over NFSv4.1 for namespace, attributes, and locking, and it talks directly to data servers for the actual I/O.

    Figure 17.    pNFS client session workflow.

    1. When a pNFS client opens a file, it sends an NFSv4.1 ‘OPEN’ and ‘GETATTR’ to the MDS which returns a filehandle and any required state.
    1. The client then issues a ‘LAYOUTGET’ to the MDS, which responds with a layout describing exactly which Data Servers (DSs) hold which byte ranges or stripes of the file, often using a ‘files’ layout with per-node NFS file-handles or device IDs. The client may also send a ‘GETDEVICEINFO’ request to which the MDS responds.
    2. For reads, once the client has this layout, it bypasses the MDS and issues NFS ‘READ’ RPCs directly to the Data Servers corresponding to the required byte ranges. The DSs return data straight to the client while the MDS is only involved again if there is a layout error or a recall, in which case the client may perform ‘LAYOUTCOMMIT’, ‘LAYOUTRETURN’, and a fresh ‘LAYOUTGET’ to resynchronize.
    3. For writes, the client similarly acquires a read-write layout via ‘LAYOUTGET’ from the MDS, then sends NFS ‘WRITE’ (and, if needed, ‘COMMIT’) operations directly to the Data Servers based on the stripe mapping in the layout.
    4. After the Data Servers have durably stored the data, the pNFS client uses ‘LAYOUTCOMMIT’ to inform the MDS about changes such as the updated file size and modification time. 
    5. Finally, the client passes a ‘LAYOUTRETURN’ when it is finished with the layout.

    Throughout this process, all metadata operations, including directory lookups, creates, deletes, renames, attribute changes, and locks, are handled exclusively by the MDS using standard NFSv4.1 operations (i.e. LOOKUP, CREATE, REMOVE, RENAME, GETATTR, SETATTR, LOCK, and LOCKU, etc). In contrast, the Data Servers never see namespace, simply serving or accepting data for extents identified by the layout. The net effect is that metadata and control traffic (opens, layouts, locks) flow between the client and the MDS, while bulk data reads and writes flow directly between the client and multiple DS nodes in parallel, allowing the data path to scale with the number of storage nodes rather than being bottlenecked by a single NFS server.

    The primary benefits of pNFS include increased single‑client throughput by eliminating the single‑node bottleneck and distributing I/O across all nodes within a SmartConnect pool, as well as improved aggregate cluster throughput through more balanced I/O distribution and better utilization of existing caching and prefetch mechanisms. This functionality is transparent to applications, as pNFS negotiation occurs automatically between the Linux NFS client and the OneFS NFS server without requiring application‑level changes. Because OneFS provides a single distributed filesystem in which every node inherently has access to all data, pNFS simply authorizes the client to communicate directly with additional nodes for data transfer.

    When a pNFS‑capable client mounts an NFS export on a pNFS‑enabled OneFS cluster, each node functions as both a Metadata Server and a Data Server, with the Metadata Server role being implicitly assigned to the node the client initially contacts during the mount. Data I/O operations are performed using NFSv3, as permitted by the pNFS Flexible File Layout specification, while NFSv4.1 or NFSv4.2 is used exclusively for layout management and metadata operations. Layouts are granted on a per‑file basis, with the client requesting a layout upon file open that specifies the appropriate data server or servers for that file. Different files may be assigned to different nodes, and traffic distribution behavior is influenced by server‑side alignment settings. The set of data server addresses provided to the client is determined by the SmartConnect pool associated with the mount IP address.

    The OneFS NFSv4.1 or v4.2 metadata server (MDS) conducts all metadata and control operations over TCP port 2049. As part of the layout, the MDS returns the data server (DS) network addresses and file handles directly to the client, eliminating the need for the auxiliary mount (mountd) and portmapper (rpcbind) services. The MDS also manages all locking and state, so the Network Lock Manager (lockd) and Network Status Monitor (statd) services are not required. Clients perform NFSv3 data-path I/O directly to the DS nodes over TCP port 2049 and, in the event of a DS node failure, transparently fall back to the MDS over the same port.

    To activate pNFS, the cluster must be running OneFS 9.15, with NFSv4.1 or NFSv4.2 enabled for metadata operations and NFSv3 enabled for data operations. The SmartConnect pool can use either static or dynamic IP allocation. Client systems must be running Linux kernels that support the pNFS Flexible File Layout, which is available in mainline kernels version 5.14 and later, and mounts must explicitly specify NFSv4.1 or NFSv4.2 using either TCP or RDMA transport, as UDP is not supported.

    With OneFS 9.15 and later releases, pNFS configuration can be performed via the OneFS CLI or platform API, but the WebUI does not currently have an equivalent option. Internally, the configuration is managed by the  ‘isi_gconfig’ registry keys under the NFS driver path. Client remounts are strongly recommended when enabling or disabling pNFS, as clients cache file attributes that determine layout eligibility, so may otherwise retain stale information. Activation requires unmounting NFS clients, enabling the pNFS feature from the OneFS CLI, and restarting the NFS service, with a corresponding process to disable the feature.

    Several configuration parameters control pNFS behavior, including a master enablement flag for advertising Metadata Server and Data Server capabilities, alignment settings that determine how file data is distributed across nodes, options for mapping network interfaces to pNFS devices, and internal settings governing layout tracking scalability. In particular, the stripe alignment configuration has a substantial impact on I/O distribution patterns and must be carefully considered when tuning performance, as different alignment values favor different workload characteristics.

    Table 5.      pNFS configuration parameters.

    Facet

    Details

    Layout

    Layouts are per-file. Each time a client opens a file, it requests a layout that tells it which data server to use. Different files may be assigned to different nodes. How the client spreads its traffic also depends on the server settings around alignment.

    Network

    SmartConnect determines the pool. The set of data server addresses returned to the client comes from the SmartConnect pool that the client's mount IP belongs to.

    Node roles

    Every node in the cluster acts as both a Metadata Server and a Data Server. The "MDS" role simply means the node the client happened to connect to for that mount.

    Protocol version

    Data I/O uses NFSv3. The pNFS Flexible File Layout standard allows data servers to speak NFSv3, which is well-supported and performant. The client uses NFSv4.1 only for metadata and layout management.

    As illustrated in figure 17 above, every node in the PowerScale cluster functions as both a Metadata Server (MDS) and a Data Server (DS), with the MDS role simply representing the node to which the client initially connects during the mount operation. Data I/O operations are performed using NFSv3, as permitted by the pNFS Flexible File Layout specification, while NFSv4.1 is used exclusively by the client for metadata handling and layout management. Layouts are granted on a per‑file basis, such that each time a file is opened, the client requests a layout identifying the appropriate data server, allowing different files to be serviced by different nodes, with overall traffic distribution further influenced by server‑side alignment configurations. The set of data server addresses provided to the client is determined by SmartConnect, with the addresses drawn from the SmartConnect pool associated with the client’s mount IP.

    When it comes to enabling pNFS on a PowerScale cluster, ensure that the prerequisites described in table 6 are met. These include:

    Table 6.      pNFS enablement prerequisites.

    Attribute

    Details

    OneFS version

    OneFS 9.15 or later to provide pNFS support.

    NFS protocol versions

    NFSv4.1 or NFSv4.2 must be enabled for the metadata path. NFSv3 must also be enabled for the data path. Kerberos is also supported for both the NFSv4.1 or v4.2 MDS and the NFSv3 DS nodes.

    NFSv4.1 and NFSv4.2 and can coexist with non-pNFS clients on the same export, since pNFS is negotiated individually during session setup and clients that do not support it will continue using traditional NFS I/O paths while still accessing the same files.

    SmartConnect pool type

    The SmartConnect network pool can use Static or Dynamic IP allocation.

    Client OS

    Linux with kernel pNFS Flexible File Layout support (available in mainline Linux kernel versions 5.14 and later).

    Client mount options

    The client must mount the cluster export using NFSv4.1 (-o vers=4.1) or NFSv4.2 (-o vers=4.2). Transport protocol may be RDMA (proto=rdma) or TCP (proto=tcp). UDP is unsupported.

    The process to enable pNFS support via the CLI in OneFS 9.15 and later is as follows:

    1. First, verify that the desired SmartConnect network pool is configured for static IPs:

    # isi network pools list

    1. Next, ensure that NFSv3 and NFSv4.1 are enabled:

    # isi nfs settings global view

    1. When both the above prerequisites are confirmed, pNFS can be activated:

    # isi nfs settings global modify --pnfs-enabled 1

    1. Once pNFS is successfully enabled, the cluster’s NFS exports can then be mounted from a Linux client. For example:

    # mount -t nfs4 -o vers=4.1 <pool-ip>:/ifs/data /mnt/pnfs

    1. After performing some I/O, the ‘mountstats’ file contents or CLI command output can be used to verify pNFS is active from the NFS client:

    # grep -A 20 "pnfs" /proc/self/mountstats

    Or:

    # mountstats --nfs /mnt/pnfs

    Specifically, the presence of non-zero ‘pNFS_read’ and ‘pNFS_write’ counters in the output confirms that the Linux client is using pNFS.

    Optionally, as a second part to step 3, additional optimizations and tunings can be applied if needed.

    The recommended alignment value (the default) is ‘0’

    # isi_gconfig registry.Services.lwio.Parameters.Drivers.nfs. NFSV4FFLayoutAlignedSize=0

    NIC-level device granularity configuration can also be applied via gconfig. For example:

    # isi_gconfig registry.Services.lwio.Parameters.Drivers.nfs.NFSV4LayoutDeviceUseNICAsUniqueDevice=1

    Followed by an NFS service restart:

    # isi services nfs disable && isi services nfs enable

    Additionally, if pNFS does need to be disabled for any reason, first unmount any NFS clients, then run the following CLI command:

    # isi nfs settings global modify --pnfs-enabled 0

    The OneFS pNFS implementation (and the pNFS spec in general) does not require any changes to applications, as it is negotiated transparently between the NFS client and server. This allows applications to continue reading and writing files normally while the client kernel automatically manages layout negotiation and communication with data servers.

    If a data server node becomes unavailable while a client holds a layout, the client may encounter I/O errors on the NFSv3 data path to that node. However, most Linux NFS clients will fall back to performing I/O through the metadata server (MDS) until the data server becomes available again, at which point they can re-request a layout, with the exact behavior varying by client kernel version and implementation. However, there is currently no failover support for the MDS node, since OneFS 9.15 only supports static network pools. This means that, in the event of an MDS node outage, pNFS clients will error and timeout.

    Additionally, pNFS can work with RDMA when the server advertises both TCP and RDMA data server addresses and the environment includes RDMA-capable interfaces, enabling compatible clients to use RDMA for the data path. Finally, pNFS requires NFSv3 to be enabled because the Flexible File Layout specification allows data servers to be accessed via NFSv3. The data path between clients and data server nodes uses NFSv3 for simplicity and compatibility, while the metadata operations, including layout management and file open or close operations, must use NFSv4.1 or NFSv4.2.

    The following OneFS gconfig parameters are also available for configuring and tuning pNFS if desired:

    Parameter

    Default Value

    Details

    ServerPNFSEnabled

    1

    Master on/off toggle for pNFS. Configurable via CLI, PAPI, and registry

    NFSV4FFLayoutAlignedSize

    0

    Controls stripe alignment size (registry only). Default: 0 (no striping — each file is served from a single node).

    NFSV4LayoutDeviceUseNICAsUniqueDevice

    0

    Sets device granularity in the layout (registry only). 0 = one device per node (default); 1 = one device per NIC. Not required for aggregated network interfaces.

    NFSV4LayoutTableSize

    1048576

    Internal layout hash table size (registry only). Auto-resizes at runtime. The default value suits most environments and does not typically need adjustment.

    In OneFS 9.15, pNFS has some notable considerations and caveats. These include:

    • Static SmartConnect pools required. Dynamic pool support is planned for a future release.
    • While pNFS and regular NFS clients can be mixed, pNFS clients are required to be on a static SmartConnect network pool, with non-pNFS clients on a dynamic network pool.
    • Currently, pNFS is supported via the flex-files layout only (NFSv4.1/v4.2 for metadata, NFSv3 for data). The NFSv4 files layout will be introduced in a future release.
    • The recommendation is to use Linux clients with kernel versions 5.14 or newer for pNFS.
    • The nconnect mount parameter works and forms ‘nconnect=value’ of connections per data server. There is no need to use a high value with nconnect (e.g. 32 or higher) because each DS connection will form with “value” number of connections
    • OneFS pNFS works with both TCP and RDMA network transports.
    • The recommendation is to retain the default stripe alignment (AlignedSize) parameter configuration value of ‘0’.
    • No server-initiated layout recall (CB_LAYOUTRECALL). Server cannot revoke layouts and clients return them voluntarily.
    • No layout persistence across NFS restarts. Clients must re-request layouts after service or node restart.
    • No pool change notifications. To refresh pool membership cache, restart NFS.
    • Read/write size is fixed at 1 MB on the data path. Client-reported I/O errors are not processed by the server.

Home > Storage > PowerScale (Isilon) > White Papers > Dell PowerScale: OneFS NFS Design Considerations and Best Practices > SmartConnect

SmartConnect

  • SmartConnect, a licensable software module of the PowerScale OneFS operating system, helps to greatly simplify client management across the enterprise. Through a single host name, SmartConnect enables client connection load balancing and dynamic NFS failover and failback of client connections across storage nodes to provide optimal utilization of the cluster resources.

    Client Connection Load Balancing

    SmartConnect balances client connections across nodes based on policies that ensure optimal use of cluster resources. By leveraging your existing network infrastructure, SmartConnect provides a layer of intelligence that allows all client and user resources to point to a single hostname, enabling easy management of a large and growing numbers of clients. Based on user configurable policies, SmartConnect applies intelligent algorithms (CPU utilization, aggregate throughput, connection count, or round robin) and distributes clients across the cluster to optimize client performance and end-user experience. SmartConnect can be configured into multiple zones that can be used to ensure different levels of service for different groups of clients. All of this is transparent to the end user.

    NFS failover using dynamic IP pool

    SmartConnect uses a virtual IP failover scheme that is specifically designed for PowerScale scale-out NAS storage and does not require any client-side drivers. The PowerScale cluster shares a “pool” of virtual IPs that is distributed across all nodes of the cluster. The cluster distributes an IP address across NFS (Linux and UNIX) clients based on a client connection balancing policy.

    This is an example illustrating how NFS failover works. As shown in Figure 2, in the six-node OneFS cluster, an IP address pool provides a single static node IP (10.132.0.140 – 10.132.0.145) to an interface in each cluster node. Another pool of dynamic IPs (NFS failover IPs) has been created and distributed across the cluster (10.132.0.150 – 10.132.0.161).

    Figure 2.   Dynamic IPs and Static IPs

    When Node 1 in the cluster goes offline, the NFS failover IPs and connected clients associated with Node 1 failover to the remaining nodes based on the configured IP failover policy (Round Robin, Connection Count, Network Throughput, or CPU Usage). The static IP for Node 1 is no longer available as shown in Figure 3.

    Figure 3.   NFS Failover with Dynamic IP Pool

    Therefore, using dynamic IP pool for NFS workload is recommended to provide NFS service resilience. If a node with client connections established goes offline, the behavior is protocol-specific. Because NFSv3 is a stateless protocol, after the node failure, workflows can be moved easily from one cluster node to another. It will automatically reestablish the connection with the IP on the new interface and retries the last NFS operation. NFSv4.x is a stateful protocol, the connection state between the client and the node is maintained by OneFS to support NFSv4.x failover and in OneFS 8.x versions and higher, OneFS keeps that connection state information for NFSv4.x synchronized across multiple nodes. Once the node failure occurs, the client can resume the workflow with the same IP on the new node using the previous maintained connection state.

    The number of IPs available to the dynamic pool directly affects how the cluster load balances the failed connections.  For small clusters under N (N<=10) nodes, the formula N*(N-1) will provide a reasonable number of IPs in a pool. For larger clusters, the number of IPs per pool is between the number of nodes and the number of clients. Requirements for larger clusters are highly dependent on the workflow and the number of clients.

SmartQoS overview

  • SmartQoS allows administrators to apply an OPS ceiling or limit to specified workloads for business workload prioritization: SmartQoS:

    • Is applicable to NFSv3, NFSv4, NFSoRDMA, SMB, and S3 
    • Enables IT infrastructure teams to achieve performance SLAs
    • Enables throttling of rogue or low-priority workloads, thus prioritizing other business-critical workloads
    • Helps minimize DU events due to overloaded clusters

Step 1: Confirm the cluster pool

  • On the PowerScale cluster, examine the SmartConnect static network pool to obtain the exact IP range and gateway that the client will route across its two NICs:

    # on the cluster

    isi network pools list

    isi network subnets list

    You will mount one address from this range (or the pool’s SmartConnect DNS name, which resolves to one of them) and route the entire range across your two NICs.

    Caution: Use the NFS data pool, not the management pool. A management or pool0 address may answer ping and even accept a TCP connection on port 2049, but mounts through it hang and never produce data layouts. Choose the pool on the cluster’s data interfaces (for example, 25/100 GbE), and split exactly that pool’s range.

Step 2: Back up the current network configuration

  • Before changing anything, capture the current state so you can restore it. First, on the Linux client, save the runtime routing state (all distributions):

    mkdir -p /root/net-backup-$(date +%F)

    ip route show > /root/net-backup-$(date +%F)/routes.txt

    ip rule show  > /root/net-backup-$(date +%F)/rules.txt

    Next, back up the persistent network configuration for your distribution on the client. This is only required if you will use Option B (permanent routes) in Step 3; Option A leaves persistent configuration untouched.

    • NetworkManager (RHEL, Rocky, SLES): profiles live in /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/ (keyfile) or /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ (ifcfg). Back up whichever is present.
    • netplan (Ubuntu): back up /etc/netplan.

    # Ubuntu / netplan example

    cp -a /etc/netplan /root/net-backup-$(date +%F)/

    Tip: Keep these backups until the new configuration is confirmed working and stable.

Step 3: Add the split routes

  • Add a host-specific (/32) route for every pool address, sending half to each NIC. There are two ways to accomplish this.

    Option A — Temporary (runtime only, for testing)

    These routes take effect immediately and are lost on reboot, which makes them ideal for validating the configuration before committing. On the Linux client, run the following as root:

    # .81–.100 via NIC 1

    for id in {81..100}; do

      ip route replace 192.168.100.$id via 10.10.1.254 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.11

    done

    # .101–.120 via NIC 2

    for id in {101..120}; do

      ip route replace 192.168.100.$id via 10.10.2.254 dev eth1 src 10.10.2.11

    done

    ip route flush cache

    The src attribute pins the connection’s source address to the egress NIC. It is required for RDMA (the RoCE source GID must belong to the egress device) and keeps the path symmetric. Because ip route replace is idempotent, the commands are safe to re-run.

    Option B — Permanent (choose one method)

    Store the routes declaratively so the network stack reapplies them automatically on boot or NIC bounce. Choose one method; do not combine them for the same addresses.

    NetworkManager (RHEL, Rocky, SLES). On the client, add the routes with nmcli, using the connection name (from nmcli connection show), which often differs from the device name. The src attribute pins the source address exactly as in Option A.

    nmcli connection show    # note the NAME column (may differ from DEVICE)

    # NIC 1 connection

    for id in {81..100}; do

      nmcli connection modify eth0 \

        +ipv4.routes "192.168.100.$id/32 10.10.1.254 src=10.10.1.11"

    done

    # NIC 2 connection (name may be e.g. "Wired connection 1")

    for id in {101..120}; do

      nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" \

        +ipv4.routes "192.168.100.$id/32 10.10.2.254 src=10.10.2.11"

    done

    nmcli connection up eth0

    nmcli connection up "Wired connection 1"

    Caution: nmcli connection up briefly bounces the interface and drops any SSH session running over that NIC. Run the activation from the console/BMC, or detached (for example, wrap it in nohup ... &). Do not chain the two commands with && over a live SSH session on the first NIC.

    Ubuntu / netplan. On the client, add routes under each interface in the netplan YAML, then run sudo netplan apply. A route placed under an interface egresses that interface and uses its IP as the source automatically, so no explicit src is needed. Validate with ‘sudo netplan generate’ before applying.

    network:

      version: 2

      ethernets:

        eth0:

          routes:

            - to: 192.168.100.81/32

              via: 10.10.1.254

            # ... one entry per .81–.100

        eth1:

          routes:

            - to: 192.168.100.101/32

              via: 10.10.2.254

            # ... one entry per .101–.120

    OS-agnostic — systemd oneshot service. For mixed client fleets, or when a single approach across all hosts is preferred, this small ‘oneshot service’ replays the Option A commands at boot on the client. It is the most transparent method, and the safest to apply remotely, because it never reconfigures a NIC’s address and so never bounces a link.

    # /usr/local/sbin/nfs-trunk-routes.sh

    #!/bin/bash

    set -e

    for id in {81..100}; do

      ip route replace 192.168.100.$id via 10.10.1.254 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.11

    done

    for id in {101..120}; do

      ip route replace 192.168.100.$id via 10.10.2.254 dev eth1 src 10.10.2.11

    done

    ip route flush cache

    # /etc/systemd/system/nfs-trunk-routes.service

    [Unit]

    Description=Split NFS pool routes for NIC trunking

    After=network-online.target

    Wants=network-online.target

    [Service]

    Type=oneshot

    RemainAfterExit=yes

    ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/nfs-trunk-routes.sh

    [Install]

    WantedBy=multi-user.target

    chmod +x /usr/local/sbin/nfs-trunk-routes.sh

    systemctl daemon-reload

    systemctl enable --now nfs-trunk-routes.service

    systemctl status nfs-trunk-routes.service --no-pager  # expect: active (exited)

    Note: On-link pool (no gateway) is a special case. If the cluster pool is in the same subnet as your client NICs — shown by ip route show as a proto kernel scope link route with no via — omit the gateway: For example, ip route replace 192.168.100.81 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.11, or in netplan use scope: link with no via. When the pool is reached through a router, keep the gateway.

Step 4: Verify the split

  • On the Linux client, confirm that the boundary addresses resolve to the expected interfaces:

    ip route get 192.168.100.81    # expect: dev eth0  src 10.10.1.11

    ip route get 192.168.100.100   # expect: dev eth0  src 10.10.1.11

    ip route get 192.168.100.101   # expect: dev eth1  src 10.10.2.11

    ip route get 192.168.100.120   # expect: dev eth1  src 10.10.2.11

    Or check the whole pool at once:

    for id in {81..120}; do ip route get 192.168.100.$id | head -1; done

    Addresses .81–.100 should all show eth0, and .101–.120 should all show eth1.

Step 5: Connectivity check (optional)

  • On the Linux client, perform a quick reachability check before mounting. Skip it if you prefer to go straight to Step 6 — the mount plus the verification in Steps 7 and 8 is the definitive end-to-end test.

    # RDMA only: both devices should be ACTIVE / LINK_UP

    rdma link show

    # reach one IP from each half over its intended NIC

    ping -c2 -I eth0 192.168.100.81      # path via NIC 1

    ping -c2 -I eth1 192.168.100.101     # path via NIC 2

    A ping failure on one NIC means that path is down — check link state, switch/VLAN configuration, and gateway reachability (for example, arping -I eth1 10.10.2.254).

Home > Storage > PowerScale (Isilon) > White Papers > Dell PowerScale: OneFS NFS Design Considerations and Best Practices > Step 6: Mount

Step 6: Mount

  • On the Linux client, mount one pool address as the MDS, using nconnect to set the number of connections opened per DS address:

    For RDMA configurations:

    mount -v -o proto=rdma,port=20049,vers=4.1,rsize=1048576,wsize=1048576,nconnect=4 \

      192.168.100.81:/ifs/data /mnt/pscale/

    For TCP configuration:

    Replace 'proto=rdma,port=20049' with 'proto=tcp'

    The mount confirms the source address it selected. The reported clientaddr should match your NIC 1 IP (10.10.1.11).

    Note: Immediately after mounting, and before any I/O, only the MDS address appears in the transport table. This is expected — DS connections are created once I/O triggers LAYOUTGET.

    To remount automatically on boot, add an entry to /etc/fstab on the client (_netdev defers the mount until the network is up):

    192.168.100.81:/ifs/data  /mnt/pscale  nfs4  \

      proto=rdma,port=20049,vers=4.1,rsize=1048576,wsize=1048576,nconnect=4,_netdev  0  0

Step 7: Verify trunking — transport connections

  • On the client, generate a small amount of I/O (for example, a find, or a short fio or dd job) to trigger layout retrieval, then count the transport connections per address:

    grep -h 'addr:' /sys/kernel/debug/sunrpc/rpc_xprt/*/info \

      | awk '{print $2}' | sort -t. -k4 -n | uniq -c

    Healthy trunking shows every participating address with nconnect (here, 4) connections — the MDS plus DS addresses from both halves of the pool:

      4 192.168.100.81     <- MDS (NIC 1 range)

      4 192.168.100.90     <- DS  (NIC 1 range)

      4 192.168.100.101    <- DS  (NIC 2 range)

      4 192.168.100.118    <- DS  (NIC 2 range)

      ...

    If only .81–.100 appear, the NIC 2 routes are wrong — recheck Step 4. Entries for the cluster management address (port 2049) and the local rpcbind socket are unrelated to data I/O and can be ignored.

Step 8: Verify trunking — RDMA queue pairs (RDMA only)

  • For RDMA configurations, on the Linux client, confirm that queue pairs (QPs) exist on both RDMA devices:

    rdma resource show qp link mlx5_0    # NIC 1

    rdma resource show qp link mlx5_1    # NIC 2

    Both devices must return QPs, and each should carry roughly half of the total — for a 40-address pool with nconnect=4, about 20 × 4 = ~80 QPs per device. QPs on only one device mean all traffic is on one NIC; recheck the routes for the other half.

    Tip: If you validated with temporary routes (Option A) and everything checks out, return to Step 3, Option B to make the routes permanent.

Summary of NIC trunking

  • Client-side NIC trunking is an efficient, fully reversible way to unlock the aggregate bandwidth of two client interfaces for pNFS flex-files on Dell PowerScale. Because the technique relies only on host-specific routes and an ‘nconnect’ mount, it requires no cluster-side change and applies equally to RDMA and TCP. Following the procedure in this guide (i.e. confirm the correct data pool, back up first, split the routes, verify with the transport and queue-pair checks, and persist with a tested rollback in place) delivers a single mount that drives data traffic across both NICs.

The single-NIC limitation

  • By default, Linux resolves all of those DS addresses to a single egress interface — the route with the lowest metric wins — so every data connection leaves through one NIC. A client with two NICs attached to the same PowerScale data network therefore uses only half of its available bandwidth, while the second NIC stays idle.

    Figure 25.    Default single-NIC behavior (left) versus client-side NIC trunking (right).

Home > Storage > PowerScale (Isilon) > White Papers > Dell PowerScale: OneFS NFS Design Considerations and Best Practices > The trunking solution

The trunking solution

  • The technique in this guide pins half of the pool’s addresses to each NIC using host-specific (/32) routes. Data-server connections then fan out across both interfaces, so a single mount can drive the aggregate bandwidth of both NICs. The approach works identically for RDMA (RoCE/InfiniBand) and TCP; RDMA-only steps are marked where they apply. All configuration is performed on the Linux client; the cluster requires no change beyond having NFS over RDMA and pNFS flex-files enabled on the export.

Troubleshooting NIC trunking

  • Table 11.  Common symptoms, causes, and resolutions

    Symptom

    Likely cause

    Resolution

    Ping or mount hangs on one NIC’s path

    No working path via that NIC’s gateway

    Check link, switch/VLAN, and gateway (arping -I eth1 10.10.2.254)

    Mount hangs though ping and port are reachable

    Mounting the wrong pool (management, not data)

    Confirm the IP is in the NFS data pool (isi network pools list); mount a data-pool IP

    Only NIC 1 addresses in the transport table

    NIC 2 host routes missing or wrong

    Recheck ip route get 192.168.100.101

    No QPs on mlx5_1

    RDMA device not mapped to NIC 2

    rdma link show; confirm device-to-netdev mapping

    Transport table shows only the MDS IP after I/O

    pNFS flex-files inactive, or no real I/O performed

    Confirm flex-files is enabled on the export; perform real reads/writes

    ip route get shows the wrong NIC

    Route cache stale

    ip route flush cache

    SSH session drops during Option B apply/rollback

    nmcli connection up bounced the NIC carrying your session

    Run the activation detached (nohup ... &) or from console/BMC

    Routes still present after Option B rollback

    cp -a keyfile restore did not delete an NM-created profile

    Use the -ipv4.routes rollback method; verify with ip route show

    ip route replace permission error

    Not root

    Use sudo
